newsitem.title: USA: Kyrgyz officials upbeat on IMF, growth prospects.
newsitem.headline: Kyrgyz officials upbeat on IMF, growth prospects.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Kyrgyzstan hopes for new International Monetary Fund loans when a three-year deal expires this year but has no plans to tap international markets, officials said on Tuesday.
Central Bank Chairman Marat Sultanov told a news conference that impoverished Kyrgyzstan was looking for IMF funds or concessionary credits.
"While it is possible to get credits like that, we will not be looking at Eurobonds," he said. "If we get richer we can use other resources."

He told Reuters after the news conference that Kyrgyzstan expected gross domestic product to rise almost seven percent next year, after some 6.5 percent this year. Inflation would fall to 10 percent, from a forecast 17 percent in 1997.
"Our main task by the year 2000 is to do things so that economic growth will be higher than inflation," he said.
Kyrgyzstan, heavily dependent on budget handouts from Moscow during Soviet days, was one of the first former Soviet republics to embrace market-oriented reforms.

But the landlocked Central Asian country has few natural resources, with the exception of a big gold mining project, and GDP per capita is less than $650 a year. Russia's GDP per capita, by contrast, is almost $3,000.
Sami Geadah, IMF mission chief for Kyrgyzstan, told Reuters earlier that the Kyrgyz economy was doing well.

"Inflation is down, growth has picked up, the fiscal deficit is being reduced, interest rates are coming down, the exchange rate is stable and reserves are up," he said. "There are structural reforms, for example on privatisation.
"That is not to say that they will have a fully funtioning mket economy -- there is still a lot to be done in terms of stability and structual reform. But overall things have been going quite well."
He said a successor to the current IMF deal was already under discussion.
